items.text: The default g's lower loop is rebuilt, as you asked me to confirm. You were right: in 0.80 its left side was a nearly straight stroke ending in a knob that overlapped the link, and in the variable font the overlap left a white sliver at 550 and 700. Now the loop is four quarters at the bowl's tensions, its left side meets the link as a branch (the same 32-unit neck as every other branch), and its counter is a contour of its own. Curvature runs smoothly round it (worst ratio across a node 1.13, was 1.56).

One tail family. The single-storey g's tail is a half-ellipse: both edges leave the stem at the ball's height, the lowest point half way to the tail's end, the ball 0.030 of the x-height under the baseline. j's and y's tails and the a's curled exit now follow the same rule: from the stem round the lowest point to the ball the curve only tightens, and it is equal on both sides of the lowest point. In the Bold the g's ball rises only as far as the white between it and the bowl keeps the white law (it fell to 38 units at 700; now 52).

The alternates are in the font, each in its own stylistic set: footless 1 (ss01), single-storey g (ss02), single-storey a with its 31 accented forms (ss03; four constructions were drawn and the one whose width is the references' share of n was chosen), tailed l (ss04), slashed zero (zero), dotted zero (ss05), barred 7 and z (ss06). They exist at every weight.

Letters with a stroke through them (Ł Ø Đ Ħ Ⱥ ₩ ₦ and 52 others) are, in the variable font, the letter plus the stroke as two overlapping shapes, so nothing has to be re-cut between weights. The static Regular is unchanged. Where a stroke would lie exactly along the letter's own edge (Ɍ in the Light, for 74 units) it now stops where that edge begins, so no seam can show. Ⱥ and the T with a diagonal stroke still fill their small pocket of white at the Bold: that is your decision (figure 9: keep the honest overlap, or cut the stroke inside the letter).

Signs made of arms (asterisk, daggers, exclamation, straight quotes) are now each arm's centre line with its width profile, thickened by one number per weight, and drawn symmetric from one half. The asterisk no longer looks nearly Regular in Bold text: its arms reach a little further at the Bold (6.5% longer, inside the references' own range of 1.7% to 9.2%), so the white between its balls allows them their weight. Its ink now gains 0.82 of n's gain, as Georgia Pro's does (0.819; Source Serif 4 0.898, Literata 0.935; it was 0.74). The longer arm no longer bends its curves: the outer part of each arm, from its first smooth node out to its tip, moves out whole. The Light's asterisk is 1.7% shorter, as the references' are, and unchanged.

The weight axis is now checked exactly over the whole range, not at 25-unit stops, and a second method measures every stroke across itself on the variable font. New rules from what they found: along a tapering stroke (a tail, a hook, a flag) each place keeps the share of its thickness its kind keeps (a stem's place the stem's, a hairline's place the hairline's, in between in proportion), so eng's tail no longer thins faster than its stem; a crotch with one straight side keeps its neck towards the Light; a mirrored pair (⇤ ⇥) is one drawing at every weight; an S's turn drawn at a node stays at that node. White between two parts is held like a counter. 434 of 434 parts are on target at the Light and the Bold.

Kerning is fitted per weight. Each master's pairs come from its own outlines by one rule measured on Georgia Pro and Serrif: a pair's white scales with the control white (nn, HH) of that weight. Then each is compared with the references at the same weight and opened where two letters come too close. AV goes -83 / -79 / -93 at 300 / 400 / 700 where it was -79 at every weight. The Regular's own pairs were measured again on the new letters: 772 of 4,796 measured pairs moved, most by a unit; the largest (15 to 19) are r before round letters, capitals and punctuation: r's outline has not changed since 0.80, but measured afresh it stood 8 or more units looser than both references beside those letters, so the fit brought it in. Why the stored values missed this is not known.

@ in the Bold: its a has a slanted stem (one side straight, the other the counter's edge), which the weight engine did not read as a stroke, so the stem stayed as thin as the Regular's while the counter slid into the bowl's lower stroke (29 down to 17 units at 550). The stem now thickens like every stem and the bowl stays open (at least 33 units from 550 to 700). A word space before j read tight because j's tail runs under it (the white across 's j' was 252 units where Georgia Pro has 322); the space before j is now kerned by the measured shortfall (s j 302 at 400), the only change to the Regular. The weight checks now measure a stroke across itself rather than along a level or upright line (the comma below a capital passes: it never thinned), and no longer read a terminal's cut end or a junction as a stroke. The figure of signs and struck glyphs showed some glyphs as other glyphs; that was the figure tool, not the font, and it is fixed.

The hook above (on Ả ẩ ỉ ở and 23 more) is now built in the weights as a curl and a stem that overlap, as the struck letters are: its small eye keeps its width and the curl grows outward, so the capital form no longer crosses itself from 550 in the Bold. In the Bold, @'s top crotch no longer rises above its stem (a nub), and C's lower barb no longer thins where it meets the bowl (the tapering rule had lengthened one handle there). The weight checks now compare a stroke with the same place in the Regular, which showed that C, Q, s and the capital ogonek never thinned (it was where the check's sampling fell) and found other places that do thin in the Bold: the ring of ® by R's leg, @'s a, K with hook, ₵, and the footless 1's flag. The second check reads straight strokes again (dashes, arrows, maths signs, v, w had gone unread). The Regular is unchanged.

The tails of j and y (and ȷ, ŋ, the fj ligatures, and g.ss02, which is built from j) are now built again in the Bold instead of being stretched by the weight engine (the Light's were already smooth and stay). The ball is the same part as the round ends of a c f r 2 3 5 6 9: the Regular's ball scaled evenly (1.40 at the Bold), so it stays round; the Bold j's ball had come out 61 by 49 units, pinched. The tail between the stem and the ball is solved again by the Regular's own rule, so its curvature only rises toward the ball. Where two curves meet in the masters' tails and loops they now meet at one curvature (the Bold g's loop was 1.87 times, j 1.80, the alternate a 1.76, the tailed l 1.91), never at the stroke's expense. The curvature check now runs on the Light and Bold masters too.

The single-storey g's tail is back to 0.80's proportions: the ball's top 0.138 of the x-height under the baseline (72 units, as 0.80; 0.81 had raised it to 16), the tail ending where both had it, with 0.81's smooth half-ellipse kept (no curvature fault in any master). The white between the ball and the bowl keeps its law at the Bold.

A new check measures, for every letter and figure from 300 to 700, how far its top half's ink drifts sideways against its bottom half, the drift of its centre, the stress angle of each counter and whether both sides of a round thicken alike, against Georgia Pro and Source Serif 4. The x leaned most: its thick diagonal turned 6 degrees flatter at the Bold (the references turn at most 2) and the x grew 24% wider (references 5 to 16%). Keeping the thick diagonal's slant fixes the lean (-0.123 to -0.043 of its height, the references -0.037 to -0.018) but bent the x's serif brackets between the weights, because the serifs are placed separately from the stroke; it is not in this build and needs the serifs placed from the stroke first. The 9's lower right (and the 6's upper left, the same drawing turned) is steeper than both references in the Regular already (19 degrees against 24 to 26 from its widest point down), because its tail's lowest point sits too far right for the 9's narrow width; that is a drawing decision left to you, not changed.

The 9's lower right is fuller: its lowest point moved left and its ball sits under the bowl's left side, so the right edge leans 24 degrees as in Georgia Pro and Source Serif 4 instead of 18; the 6 is the same drawing turned. The 5's upright stroke stands straighter (5 degrees, was 9.5), which is what read as italic; its bowl was already in line with the references. In the Bold the default g's loop, the alternate a and the tailed l now meet at one curvature without thinning. A fix for the x's lean at the Bold worked on the x but narrowed its openings and thinned the ampersand, so it is not in this build. A table of how each part thickens shows balls, necks, serif tips and stems growing evenly; s's turns, g's ear, the x's and w's thick strokes and Z's level strokes grow faster than their kind.

Not finished. In the Light the default g's loop still meets at uneven curvature (smoothing it would thin the stroke). The x and s, z, G, S, X, e, g, w, a, c lean further than Georgia Pro and Source Serif 4 as the weight rises (the x most). The x, s, z, G, S, X, e, g, w, a and c still lean further than both references at the Bold. Hooks ending in a ball (ⱳ ƴ Ƙ Ⱳ Ƴ ɲ ƒ, and j and eng) thin a little faster than the stems in the Light; they need a construction of their own, not built. @ in the Light: its a's stem thickens slightly (95 against 92); a fix tried this round ran the counter into the bowl and was not kept. Places that thin in the Bold, found by the same-place check and not yet fixed: ®'s ring by R's leg, @'s a, K with hook, ₵, t with retroflex hook, the footless 1's flag. ⌦ ⌫ ✓ thin faster than other signs in the Light. Junction places in Ə ɂ & $ ð œ and ɽ's ball are still flagged by the second check. Ⱥ and the T with a diagonal stroke wait for your decision (figure 9).

The single-storey g's tail (stylistic set 2) is redrawn. What was wrong: it was still j's hook with its points slid sideways. The inside ran level for 70 units and then turned up into the ball within 41 units of height, and the ball sat as low as j's, so the tail read as a flat tray with a knob on the end. Now the tail is its own part: four quarter turns between the stem, the lowest point and the ball, each a true quarter of an ellipse, so nothing in it is level or straight. The ball's top is raised to where the three references with this letter have it (0.14 of the x-height under the baseline; it was 0.19) and the tail is as thin at the bottom as theirs (0.96 of the round letters' hairline; it was 1.10). In the Bold the ball rises a little more and the lowest point moves left, as Source Serif's and Literata's Bold do, so the inside stays round.

One dollar: the ball-end one you prefer. It is now the default and stylistic set 3 is gone. The S-with-barbs dollar I built in 0.71 is removed; the stroke through the new one is the same hairline as before.

Serifs, examined one by one at five weights. I measured every foot serif and flag of the letters (tip, reach, thickness half way in, where the bracket ends) at 300, 400, 500, 600 and 700. Result: every true serif of a kind has the same tip and the same bracket at every weight, within half a unit, and they scale as the references' do (tip 0.77 of the Regular's at Light and 1.36 at Bold; four open references run 0.71 to 0.87 and 1.12 to 1.51). One real fault turned up: the bracket under the flag of n and k was drawn as two curves where every other flag has one, so those two flags stood 74 tall at the stem against 92 on i, m, p, r, u, b, d, h and l, at every weight. Both now have the same single curve. f, p and q keep their longer bowl-side foot and r its long right foot; those are earlier decisions, not faults.

There is a Light now, and the weight slider runs from 300 to 700. It is made the way the Bold is: the Regular's own points moved by the same rules, run below the Regular instead of above it. The numbers come from six faces that have a Light (Georgia Pro, Serrif, Source Serif, Literata, Newsreader, Merriweather), Light over Regular: stems 0.70, so Area's stem goes from 78 to 55; hairlines 0.82; serif tips 0.82; the dot of i 0.78; letters stay almost as wide (0.98). One thing differs from the Bold: towards the Bold thin strokes barely gain, but towards the Light they give up nearly as much as the stems, so contrast holds. Every letter and figure is on its target (415 parts of 415). Outside the letters it is not finished: see the list under this.

Not finished along the weight axis. Bold side, unchanged from 0.79: 18 glyphs gain an inflection (x among them), 18 gain a crossing, 30 have a part thinner than the Regular's (24 are accents' thin ends). Light side, new: 8 glyphs gain an inflection or a crossing (Ⱥ, †, ₩, the hooked G and W, the L with a tilde, ⌃) and 18 have a part that thins more than a serif tip does (the asterisk, small 6 and 9, ™ and ℠, the two daggers, the comma accent). Four glyphs still have no real Bold (Ⱥ † ₡ ⌘) and six no real Light (₡, the four diagonal arrows, one combining comma). The Light's kerning is the Regular's; it is not fitted. The Light was checked at 300 by parts; the weights between 300 and 400 were checked for kinks, crossings and thin strokes on every glyph but not part by part.

Alternate candidates are drawn but not in the font: a single-storey a (q's top on d's foot), an l with a tail (l's stem on t's hook), a slashed zero, a dotted zero, a barred 7 and a barred z. The figure shows each beside the default, large and at 16 px. I went through the whole list you pasted, letter by letter, in docs/research/serif-typeface-2026-11-10/alternates-2026-11-14.md: most of it is italic or display forms that do not help interface text. My order if you want any built: slashed zero, then the single-storey a as the partner of the g, then the tailed l.

Soft corners, the option you picked, is built. Every plain stroke outside the letters now ends on the same small radius the letters' cut ends have (7): the hyphen and dashes, minus, plus, equals, underscore, bar, both slashes and the fraction bar, the arrows, the square brackets' arms, and the bars struck through letters and currency signs (ł đ ħ € ₩ and the rest). 155 glyphs, 370 ends, Regular and Bold. A corner where two strokes meet, like the inside of the plus, stays sharp. At 13 to 16 px you will not see it; at headline sizes the signs stop being the only square-cornered things in a line.

You were right about the S. I measured the alternate S and s against the default ones: both end in the same cut barbs, the spine is the same weight (95 and 96, 85 and 85), and the only real differences were width (S 5 units narrower of 489, s 55 of 379) and slightly sharper barbs. That is proportion, not form, so both are removed. The dollar is different in form: Libre Baskerville's ends in balls where the default ends in barbs. It stays, alone, and stylistic set 3 is now called Ball-end dollar.

The single-storey g (stylistic set 2) is rebuilt. What was wrong: I had cut q level at the baseline to take its top, and that sliced off the bottom of the bowl, which dips 10 units under the line. So the bowl stood on a flat 138 units long. That was the flat bottom you saw. The tail was also just j's narrow hook. The three faces I could measure that have this letter (Serrif, Source Serif, Literata) all use their q's whole bowl and run the tail under the whole of it, ending 0.93 to 0.97 of the bowl's width to the left; Area's ended at 0.66. Now the bowl is q's, whole, and the tail is j's stem, thickness and ball, reaching 0.96. The Bold's is put together the same way from the Bold q and j, so its bowl is no longer lighter than the q beside it.

The 5's bowl did lean. Its lowest point lay 0.37 of the way across the bowl from the left, where Georgia Pro and Serrif have 0.45 and 0.47 (and Area's own 3 has 0.45), so the bottom ran up to the right in one long slope. And the inside of the bowl was widest higher up than the outside (0.60 against 0.55 of the bowl's height; the references 0.50 against 0.53), which put the heaviest part of the stroke low on the right. Both are now at the references' mean. The ball, the upright stroke and the flag did not move. 3, 6 and 9 measured inside the references and are unchanged.

Yes, the hook should reach the i. In seven of the eight faces I measured, the fi ligature has no dot and f's hook runs 0.3 to 0.6 of a stem past the middle of the i's stem, so the end of the hook stands where the dot was. Area's fi was a plain f and a dotless i at their ordinary spacing: the hook stopped a whole stem short, with nothing over the i. Now the hook reaches 0.42 of a stem past the i's stem (Georgia Pro 0.41, Serrif 0.43), the i sits a little closer (0.885 of the distance with ligatures off, as both references), and f's bar runs into the i's flag. The same for ffi, fj and ffj. With ligatures off nothing changed: f and i measured inside the references there.

Where f's arc runs into a tall letter, the top had a 10-unit step: the bridge sat a little under the tall letter's slanted top. It is one level edge now, from the arc's highest point to the far corner of the stem. I checked every ligature for its two sides (equal to the letters set apart, in both weights; the Bold's were 4 too wide on the left and ff 22 on the right, fixed), its kerning classes (all as their letters), and looked at each at 13, 16, 32 and 100 px in Regular and Bold, on and off. ff, ft and the tall ones did not need redrawing.

The weight axis, plainly. What passes: every letter and figure is on its target at all 13 weights from 400 to 700, and the font has no incompatible glyph. What I fixed this build: curves that picked up a wobble between Regular and Bold are down from 43 glyphs to 18 (W and g are fixed; x still has one, on a serif's curve); glyphs whose outline crossed itself from 26 to 18 (the double quotes and the dots under letters no longer close up); the three capital breves no longer get lighter towards Bold. What still fails: those 18 and 18, and 30 glyphs with a part thinner than in the Regular, 24 of them the thin ends of accents (1 to 5 units). Four glyphs still have no real Bold: Ⱥ, †, ₡ and ⌘ (₩ has one now; ₡ lost its own when its bars got round ends). Not done: Bold kerning is still the Regular's opened for collisions, not fitted, and there is no measured audit yet for marks and signs in Bold. The Weight section below shows 400, 500, 600 and 700 at headline and text sizes, with the alternates.

Libre Baskerville's S, s and $ are in as alternates (stylistic set 3, font-feature-settings "ss03"). The defaults are untouched. They are the base's own drawings at Area's weight, with one change: the spine of S and s is thinned to match Area's, because the base's is a quarter heavier. Not done: the $'s spine is still the base's weight, s is narrower than Area's s, and C and G are not redrawn to match, so in this set S ends differently from C and G.

On the plain signs: seven of the eight serif faces I measured, both references among them, draw these as plain bars with square ends. I drew three options and sent the figure: soft corners (the letters' own radius), soft with a slightly heavier hyphen, and strokes that swell into their ends. I recommend the first. At 13 to 16 px all three look the same; the flared one shows only in headlines. The default is unchanged until you choose.

Your note on the return arrow's tip: yes, it needed fixing, and so did every arrow. The head was two strokes and a small triangle stuck together, which left a zigzag at the point. The head is one clean outline now. I checked every glyph for the same thing; the summation sign had a small dent, also gone.
k's right foot on the stem was 96 where every other foot is 68. It is the standard foot now, as Georgia Pro and Serrif draw theirs. r's longer foot, which you like, is untouched.

On 5 and Z leaning right: I measured them against Georgia Pro, Serrif and Libre Baskerville. The 5's flag reached further right than any of theirs, which puts weight at the top right; it ends 13 units sooner now. Its stem leans 9.5 degrees, which is Serrif's lean and what you asked for earlier, so I left it; say if you want it more upright. Z and z measure inside the three references on every lean test, so I have not changed them. The numbers are on the evaluation page.

a's bowl: I measured the stroke's thickness all the way round the counter. It swelled at the lower left, fell, held steady up the left side, then fell again, and that hold is the unevenness you saw. Changing only the lengths of the counter's handles, the swell is smaller and the change steadier (it strays 2.2 units from one smooth change, was 2.8). It is better, not perfect: removing the hold fully needs one more point on the counter, which I have not done. The same test now runs on every closed counter, and R, 6, 9, D, B and g were evened the same way.

fi is a ligature, and ligatures are on by default. The evaluation page's headline had a little letter-spacing, and browsers switch ligatures off when text is letter-spaced. That is fixed on the page. It showed a real gap too: with ligatures off, f's ball sat 13 units from the dot of i and j. They now stand 44 apart, the middle of what Georgia Pro and Serrif keep.
New: a plain, single-storey g as an alternate, made from q's bowl and stem with j's tail. Turn it on with the stylistic set ss02. It is a first version; I have not judged it in small text yet.

Not built yet, and I would rather say so: the more serif-like plus, bar, slash and dashes; Libre Baskerville's S, s and $ as alternates; and the list of other letters that could have alternates. What I found and what I would draw is on the evaluation page, at the top under Open now.

In the Bold: the two places that sat off their line between Regular and Bold (g's neck, x's thick stroke) are fixed. A new check that looks at every glyph at every weight found two real faults in bold letters, both fixed (a's bowl pinched to 11 units where it meets the stem; the foot of g's bowl to 5). That check still fails on some accents and signs.

Area Serif has a second weight. The Bold is made from the Regular's own points by rule, so the two always match point for point, and one variable font now holds every weight from 400 to 700. The Regular itself has not changed: all 1,038 glyphs are the same as in 0.75.

How heavy: stems go from 78 to 140 in the lowercase and 86 to 148 in capitals, round strokes 82 to 146, hairlines 43 to 53, serif tips 30 to 41. That keeps Area as far under Georgia Pro Bold and Serrif Bold as its Regular is under theirs. A lighter Bold with a stem of 128 is one number away and is on this page beside it, in the Weight section, so you can choose.

items.text: Slanted strokes keep their exact thickness and their taper; where two meet, the outside keeps its flat and the inside comes to a point, the way the Regular builds them. The first try made k's leg parallel-sided. The Regular's leg widens from 61 to 87, and the Bold keeps that now.

Accents follow their letters. Wedge accents (acute, grave, circumflex, caron, tilde) reach the width, height and stroke the two references' accents have in Bold. Dashes, plus, equals and brackets take measured values too.

Spacing: each letter's side bearings change by what Georgia Pro's and Serrif's change from Regular to Bold, about 5 units a side. Kerning is the Regular's, opened wherever two bold letters came closer than 13 units.

Not right yet, and I would rather say so than hide it. Ⱥ and ₩ thicken only their upright parts in Bold; their slanted strokes stay Regular weight. The dagger and ⌘ do not thicken at all. The number sign's slanted strokes come out uneven, and so do a few letters with a slash through them (₡, Ɇ). The exclamation mark's top and the guillemets are lighter than the references'. The capital breves are a little light. Bold kerning has not been fitted afresh, only opened where letters collide. Between the two weights, the neck of g's ear runs up to 2.6 units thin and x's thick stroke up to 1.8 heavy.

A mistake of mine, found late: in a dozen glyphs with a slash through them, some points landed thousands of units away, and my check did not notice because it never asked how far a point had moved. Making the font at weight 700 showed it. Fixed, and the check now fails on it.
Eng was Libre Baskerville's own N with a tail, heavier and a different width from Area's N. It is Area's N now with the tail added, as all six faces I looked at draw it. One line to change back.

My mistake in 0.71: their bars were thinned only where they cross the letter, leaving a step (49 inside, 60 to 64 outside). The whole bar is 49.

Numbers of mine that did not match their own source, corrected: lowercase accents 89 over the x-height (not 90); the eth no heavier than o; the tenge and caps lock no longer made by squashing T and the shift arrow, which had thinned their bars; the capital hook above with its counter open again; currency bars where Georgia Pro and Serrif have theirs.

Every dot outside i and j had become an oval, 7 units taller than wide. Dots are circles again. Colon, semicolon and ellipsis use the period's dot; ¡ and ¿ are ! and ? turned over; the opening quote is the closing one turned; double quotes are two singles.

The product sign's stems are H's (86, they were 74). A bracket's two arms are the same thickness. The font file's own version now says the build (it said 0.003 since the first build).

items.text: Accented letters now kern exactly as their plain letter. The kerning fixed in 0.66 had only been written for the plain letters, so K before À overlapped by 38 units while K before A was fine, and the Vietnamese letters had no kerning at all. 691 pairs with punctuation or accented letters overlapped; none does now.

The pass that keeps any two glyphs at least 13 units apart now looks at every glyph in the font, not only letters and a few punctuation marks: an accent under f's hood, j's tail under a bracket, the caron of ľ beside a tall letter.
IJ's J hung 137 units outside the glyph, so the next letter ran into it, and the numero sign's small o ran 337 units past its width. Both are rebuilt as their two parts set side by side.

These signs kept Libre Baskerville's spacing. Each side that stood off both Georgia Pro and Serrif the same way moved to the nearer one (the percent sign 26 units looser on its right, the underscore 19 tighter each side). No letter or core pair changed.

items.text: In the fractions the small figures stood almost on the bar (4 to 22 units away; in ⅔ the 2 touched it). They were made larger in 0.47 and never moved apart. Each figure now stands 66 units from the bar, what Georgia Pro and Serrif keep on average, and the bar is one width in every fraction and the percent sign.

Eight new currency signs, each Area's capital letter with bars or strokes added, like the won and ruble.

Key symbols, menu dots and solid shapes for interfaces, built from the arrows, the period's dot and plain geometry at the minus's weight. Not built, because they need your decision or parts that do not exist yet: Ŋ, ß, ẞ, escape, hooked and double arrows, ⅒, small capitals, old-style figures.

The ampersand's arm was a solid block: the white between the arm and the tail was filled in. A rule that shortens serif brackets had taken the whole underside of the arm for a bracket. The arm is a stroke again. Nothing else changed from that rule.

items.text: Accents sat off centre on letters whose width or shape Area had changed since Libre Baskerville: 42 units right on O, 41 on T, 43 on z, 27 left on s, 37 left on w. Each letter's accents now sit where Georgia Pro and Serrif put theirs. 224 accented letters follow, and typed accents too.
The plus had a thin upright on a thicker bar (40 on 52). The bar, broken bar, underscore and slash were each a different weight. All are the minus's weight now, as both references draw them.
Dollar, cent, yen and kra were still Libre Baskerville's S, c, Y and small K. They are Area's letters now with the stroke or bars added, so they match the letters and follow them.

The ring over capitals was three quarters the size of the lowercase one, its hole nearly closed at text sizes; it is the same ring now. Accents sat lower on O than on other capitals, and the capital circumflex higher than the caron; all one height.

Why those two points were sharp: my mistake in 0.65. Two edges crossed at w's middle peak and under M, and I fixed the crossing by joining the two crossed points into one, which left a point where every other vertex has a small flat. Looking at all of them, the vertices had drifted apart: the flat on the outside was 33 units on v, 23 on V and N, 19 and 20 under W, and 9, 0 and 5 on w. The inside corners were cut flat on v w M N y A but came to a point on V W x X K.

items.text: One vertex. Outside: a flat, the same share of the stem everywhere (33 units on lowercase, 36 on capitals; both references and the base design cut a flat there). Inside: a point, like every other join since 0.65. The strokes keep their exact thickness; each turns by about a degree to make room. The notches where M's and N's diagonals meet their stems are points too. A check now fails the build if any vertex drifts.

When a tip is rounded: a stroke that ENDS in a flat cut gets both corners rounded, 7 units, the same as a serif tip. That covers serif tips, bar ends (f t), beaks (E F L T Z), barbs (C G S), tail cuts. What stays sharp is anything that is a meeting of two strokes rather than an end: vertices (A M N V W v w), joins and crotches, a stem's top corner under its flag, and a cut shorter than 20 units, which is treated as a point (b's and q's spurs, 13 units, are in that last group). If you would rather the spurs were rounded, or brought to a true point, say so and I will change the rule.

Side bearings, measured optically. A new tool measures the white each side of a letter really shows (not just the distance to its serif tip) against that face's own n or H, in Area and both references. Where Area stood off both in the same direction, the side moved to the nearer one: 22 letters by 3 to 16 units. The clearest cases: I, E, F and P had their stems closer to the edge than H's (I by 8 and 9); N and M were tight; u's right side was 9 loose; B, P and G were 13 to 16 loose on the right. Hyphen and dashes were 20 a side too loose, parentheses 11 and 19 too tight.

Capitals were set tighter than both references: stem to stem across HH was 238 units where Serrif has 273 and Georgia Pro 290 (Area's serifs are shorter, so equal space at the serif tips put the stems closer). Capitals are 13 units a side looser now (HH 264), the most that keeps round capitals inside the references' range. Lowercase tracking and the word space were already inside the range and stay.

Kerning rebuilt from measurement. This found a real fault: since 0.38, pairs that the base font kerned kept the base font's old gap, while everything else took the new side bearings. So fo, fe, we, wo, ro were 25 to 90 units too tight (f nearly touched o), and iw, lw, Gw, GA were 40 to 100 too loose. I measured the white between every pair of letters and common punctuation (4,372 pairs) in all three faces. Before: 1,758 pairs stood outside both references by 8 units or more. Now: 53. Among lowercase pairs: 85 before, 5 now. 789 kerning values changed.

The smallest gap allowed between two letters is 13 units (was 22). Serrif holds 9 to 13 between serif tips and Georgia Pro lets them overlap, so 22 was pushing pairs like VV, AA and vv apart more than either. The check for near-touching pairs now also covers : ; ! ? ( ) / dashes and quotes.

Figures keep their bearings and have no kerning from this pass: Georgia Pro's default figures are old-style, so only one reference compares like for like. Qj, gj and qj stay wide apart because Area's Q tail and j's descender would collide. Checked in proofs, not in the app.

Your ten pictures, measured. Where a curved stroke meets a stem, I measured two things on every letter: whether the corner comes to a point or is cut flat, and how thick the stroke is right at the corner (the neck). Before: n h m p b d a were cut flat, 5 to 10 units wide, while r u q came to a point. The neck was 19 units on a, 22 on r, 28 on p, 29 on n h m, 34 on b, 44 on u and 62 on d's top. Georgia Pro and Serrif each hold one value on every such join, and both bring the corner to a point. So you were right on every count: these were separate drawings.

items.text: One join everywhere. The corner is now a point on the stem's edge on every letter, with no flat. The neck is 32 units on every one of them (0.41 of a stem, about three quarters of the thin stroke at the top of o; Georgia Pro's is 0.73 of its thin stroke and Serrif's 0.68). The curve leaves the stem at the same angle on all of them, 40 degrees. The height of each corner is calculated from the neck, not placed by eye. The two places where a bowl's thin stroke runs into the end of a stem (d's top, p's bottom) share a second value, 54 units, the same proportion as Georgia Pro.

The lower stroke you called way too thin was 19 units where it meets the stem, the thinnest thing in the lowercase. It is 32 now, the same as every other join, and 50 at the lowest point of the counter, the same as the top of n's arch.

One bowl. These were four drawings: the top of the bowl sat 146 to 162 units from the stem depending on the letter, and the widest point at four different heights. They now share one bowl, built once from stated numbers and mirrored. q is b turned half round and p is d turned half round, point for point; the counters are identical in all four. b's foot spur and q's head spur are the same shape turned.

u's bowl is n's arch turned half round, with u's own slightly narrower counter. Before, it was a separate, deeper curve and its join sat higher than n's. This is the most visible change in this build: please look at u in words.
r leaves its stem the way n does (same point, same neck, same angle). Its arm and ball above that are unchanged.
The stem's edge now runs straight through every join. On n, m and r the edge used to lean in toward the head serif by 4 to 15 units, and on p it stepped out 6.

The fault you saw on w. Narrowing w's thick strokes in 0.61 made two edges cross at the middle peak, leaving a sliver. I added a check that looks for any outline crossing itself; it found the same kind of 1-unit sliver on M's vertex and at notches of B, Q, g and 3 (14 glyphs with the ones built from them). All are fixed, and the check now fails the build if one appears again.

Letters built from these follow. ŋ is now n with j's tail and µ is u with a plain descender (both were still older, heavier drawings). Accented letters, đ, ħ, þ and the f ligatures picked up the new joins by themselves. I also removed 25 stray 1-unit segments from the ligatures, þ, œ and the small figures.

A new check runs with every build: each join's neck, point and angle, that the four bowls match, and that q and p are b and d turned. Any drift of more than a unit fails the build. All checks pass. Ink changed by 1.5% or less on each letter. The thick-to-thin scan from 0.64 shows no new bumps and u's fastest change fell from 0.47 to 0.34.

Not in this build, so you know: ß and the rarely used hooked letters (ɓ ɗ ɠ ɦ and similar) still carry their old joins. u's two head serifs are level while n's slope 8 degrees; both references slope u's a little, and I have left that for you to decide. The bowls of B D P R and of 6 and 9 share thin-stroke values but are not yet built from one bowl the way b d p q now are. I have checked proofs only, not the app.

Every thick-to-thin transition, checked. A new scan walks each outline in 5-unit steps and measures the stroke across at every step, on all 62 letters and figures. It looks for two things: a swell that turns back on itself (thickens, thins and thickens again by 2 units or more), and how fast a stroke changes thickness. Result: no swell turns back anywhere in the set. The fastest changes are all at ends and joins, and each is at or under Georgia Pro's rate at the same place. What it did find is below.

The two ends you asked about. y's tail narrows from its end to the thin stroke at an even 2 to 3 units per step, no dip. g's ear widens from its root to its end at an even 1 to 2 per step. Both are steady; neither needed a change. y's narrows faster than j's because its thin stroke is thinner (j 0.28 per unit, y 0.48).

The three arches had drifted apart. Where the arch leaves the stem, h's stroke was 130 units at the point n's is 111. Measured: the inside peak sat at 480, 483 and 484, the notch at 431, 439 and 430, and h's notch 6 units further out. h now takes n's arch point for point, and m takes it scaled to its narrower counters, so the transition is the same on all three.

These were not: the rounds were wider (o 6%, O 10%, c 4%, 0 5%), as were B, P, D, T, z and Z; E, F, N, U and H were narrower. Each now has Georgia Pro's proportion. Only the counter was stretched: stems, round-stroke weights, serifs and ends keep their size. Advances follow (O 875 to 794, o 640 to 608, N 788 to 850).

Shorter and blunter, toward Georgia Pro's: lowercase feet and flags 0.92 to 0.85 stems (Georgia Pro 0.78 to 0.84), capitals 0.99 to 0.94, and the tip 27 to 30 units thick (0.37 of the stem, Georgia Pro's ratio). f's and u's serifs that had not followed the others now do.

items.text: When a corner is rounded, one rule. Serif tips were rounded and every other flat-cut end was square. Now every stroke end that is cut flat has the same small round corner: beaks, barbs, bar ends, tail cuts and figure ends. What stays sharp is a point that is not an end: apexes and vertices, the top of a stem under its flag, a stem's bottom without a serif, and joins.

The typeface's rules are written down, part by part (weights, widths, serif lengths, corner rounding, round ends, curves, checks, and what is open): .claude/skills/area-type-design/references/area-serif-guidelines.md.

Weight and contrast (already lighter than Georgia Pro). Ears, hooks and round ends stay Serrif's. Not matched to Georgia Pro's width, for your call: r, g, k, x, y, K, W, X (their width is an ear, a tail or diagonals), and n, d, u, a (2 to 3% wider than Georgia Pro's; they move as one family with h, b, p, q, which already match).

Your request: an evaluation of the whole set, then a cleanup. The full evaluation, by part (serif, bracket, terminal, stem, bowl, counter, aperture and the rest), with every measurement against Serrif, Georgia Pro and Inter, is in docs/research/serif-typeface-2026-11-10/evaluation-0.32.md. What it changed is below.

items.text: Smoother curves. Where one curve arrived tight at a point and the next left flat, the arc showed a slight dent. At each such point the two handles now slide along their own line until both sides bend equally. Points and directions do not move; no handle moves more than 14 units. Dents counted across the set: 61 before, 27 now (the rest are places where a curve changes direction on purpose, such as necks into round ends and the spines of s and S).

A bug: the rule that sets the figures' bowl weight was moving the wrong side of the stroke, so it made them 10 units heavier where it was written to make them lighter (0, 6 and 9 measured 1.37 stems; capitals 1.24). This is the weight you noted on the 9 and the 5. Fixed: figure bowls are 1.17 stems, Serrif's and Georgia Pro's are 1.19. These figures are 9 to 31 units narrower.
The bar was the thinnest stroke in the face, 31 units against 46 to 56 for every other thin stroke (crossbars, arms, the o's thin). It is 46 now; its lower edge moved down, so the eye keeps its size.

Shorter serifs, one step: lowercase feet and flags from 1.00 to 0.92 stems (Serrif 0.94, Georgia Pro 0.78), capitals from 1.04 to 0.99. The inner feet of n, h and m, p's and q's descender feet (they were 1.17 to 1.40) and the r's right foot now follow the same length. Capitals are 4 to 10 units narrower; lowercase advances are unchanged.
Brackets are one curve again: on 40 of them a handle had drifted long, and on R's foot and d's flag it ran past the corner, a small bulge.
The dots were ovals (113 by 121) with uneven handles. They are circles of the same area.
Its round end comes from 1.19 stems across to 1.12, inside the family (a 1.02 to r 1.09).
Your points are where you put them. Shortening the serifs had nudged the ear's root 6 units; the fold-in now reads the r's position from its body, not its serif tips.

Weight, contrast, heights, counters and apertures already measure at the goal (stem at Inter's weight, contrast 1.64, bowls within 2 to 5 units of an ideal swell). Left for your call, in the evaluation: figure 1 and 4 stems lighter than capitals, shoulder thickness n to m, u's level head serifs, a's straight bowl top, whether serifs go shorter still.

Your note: the c was messed up. Since 0.29 the round-ends rule centred the c's end at its side point's height (425), which was level with the neck. The ball hid inside the stroke as a squat half-moon with a flat bottom, and the inner edge curled out past the neck and back in, a pinched waist. The end's centre now sits where Serrif and Georgia Pro agree, 0.75 of the x-height (Serrif 388, Georgia Pro 392; it was 425). It is the same circle as the other round ends (radius 47), and the inner edge runs straight down into the ball's inner side in one curve, as in Serrif. The point count is unchanged. The neck point and the handle you moved at 0.10 now sit on the circle.
